workouts.title: Course Overview
workouts.description: The goal of this course is to improve your foundational weightlifting skills. To do that, here's a breakdown of the equipment you'll need, how the weeks are structured, and recommended barbell loading during training sessions.

items.movement: Before starting the course, test your Snatch and Clean & Jerk by recording each lift from 3 different angles using up to 75% of your established max.
Week 1 is packed with so much important information that we've broken each day down into individual sections to make it easier to digest, find, and review.
In week 1, there are 4 training sessions covering the Snatch, Clean, Jerk and an end of week Review.

The notes at the top of each training day will highlight weights to be used. When practicing set-up up from the floor, use a barbell with a full sized plate as it better replicates starting positions than an empty bar.
There will be a coaching video at the top of each lesson, with a quick overview, and a video legend then followed by the prescribed workout including demo videos.
Each week builds off the previous so it's highly recommend to follow the course in order.
In Week 3-4, we'll focus more on the power position so using an empty barbell or one with light weight will be essential to honing in technique.
From Week 5 and on, the Clean & Jerk sessions are combined into 1, so you will only need 3 training days each week until the end of the course.
We'll be spending more time pulling from the floor, so full size plates will be key to piecing your lift together from the floor.

While we might be tempted to add on more weight here, remember the focus is on improving technique and being able to mimic the demo videos to your best of your ability, if you're unable to do that, likely your bar is too heavy.

In Week 8, the first two sessions will be review while also covering common lifting faults. In the last session, we'll revisit course testing by recording the Snatch and Clean and Jerk from 3 angles and at the same weight.

workouts.title: Week ➁ Day 1 | Snatch
workouts.description: The Power Position (also called Position 1 or the High Hang) is one of the most fundamental components to creating an efficient lift. While it looks simple, making sure you pass through it during your lift is paramount to becoming better at the snatch. ⚠ We'll spend much time paused in the Power Position in the drills to reinforce our drive is coming from our legs driving out of the dip and not bending forward and throwing the shoulders back to create momentum. workouts.title: Week ➁ Day 2 | Clean
workouts.description: Here we look at the Power Position (Position 1) in the clean. Since our clean grip is set just outside the hips, the bar will sit a lower on the thighs than with the Snatch. Unlike the snatch, where releasing the hook grip may vary from person to person depending on their overhead position, you MUST let the hook grip go as you bring the bar through to the clean receiving position. Lastly, the importance of the power position is that it drives the bar vertically with power coming from leg drive out of the dip versus leaning forward and creating momentum by driving the shoulders back. VIDEO REVIEW [1:49] Clean High Pull from Power Position [3:22] Muscle Clean from Power Position [4:06] Power Clean from Power Position Use a PVC pipe until the last movement then move to an empty barbell. Rest as needed between sets. 5 Sets x 3-5 Clean Power Position to Extension Hold Dip @2sec POP: Focus on bar and torso position with knuckles down. 5 sets x 3 Clean Dip and Shrug Hold Dip @2sec POP: Goal is to initiate with legs, reinforce pause, then shrug up - not back. 5 sets x 3 Clean High Pull from Power Position Hold Dip @2sec POP: Initiate with legs into hip/knee extension and up onto toes, relaxed arms, knuckles, elbow above wrist, arms engaged, keep bar close to body. 5 sets x 3-5 Muscle Clean from Power Position POP: From high pull add transition - High pull to shoulders, release hook grip and elbows through. 5 sets x 3-5 Power Clean from Power Position POP: From Muscle Clean with feet in receiving position and pull under into quarter squat.

workouts.description: Your introduction to the "press" progression. With each lift, pull the head back so the bar can travel straight up. Strict Press: Bar stacked on shoulders, hips and legs locked out, with elbows slightly in front and a full grip on bar. Push Press: Dip into power position to drive bar off shoulders through the legs without a redip. Push Jerk: Push down under the bar as feet slide out to receiving position. Stand bar up to finish. VIDEO REVIEW [0:35] Strict Press [2:18] Push Press [6:15] Push Jerk Perform all drills with an empty barbell. Rest as needed. 3 sets x 5 Strict Press POP: Standing tall with hips and legs locked out and bar in a solid front rack, move head out of the way, press straight up and lock out. Receive the bar back into front rack with elbows slightly in front of bar. 5 sets x 3-5 Jerk Dip Hold Dip @2 sec POP: Elbows up, torso upright, balanced in the foot, dip depth shouldn't be so deep it sacrifices torso or foot balance. 5 sets x 3 Segmented Push Press Hold Dip @2 sec POP: Dip positions from above, head moves out of the way to strong overhead finish position. workouts.title: Week ➃ Day 1 | Snatch Training
workouts.description: In weightlifting, the hang to the power position is called the 2nd Pull while the bar from the hip to the overhead receiving position is called the 3rd Pull. The key to a successful Snatch is to be super patient through the 3rd pull and allow yourself to reach full extension. ⚠ If contacting the bar is painful, likely we're not being patient enough and bringing the hips to meet the bar instead of pulling the bar to the hips. Think of the 3rd pull as being patient and allowing the bar to come to the hips and then you and bar moving up together. Lastly, struggling with depth? Receive the bar where natural and then ride the receiving position into a deeper squat. This will help you become more comfortable receiving the bar lower and lower.

workouts.description: The goal today is to move our Clean from the power / hang further and further into a squat from the hang and power position. Like the snatch, where you catch isn't as important, as making sure you finish strong by riding your receiving position into a deeper squat. As you reach the bottom of your squat, keep the chest tall with a strong front rack position with elbows high which will allow you to stand the bar up easily.

workouts.title: Week ➇ Day 1 | Common Faults 1
workouts.description: Week 8 is our opportunity to continue to dial our full lifts, review common faults and finish off the course by revisiting the testing we did at the beginning of the course. ⚠ Keep this simple, rather than trying to remember all the cues for a lift, focus on one or two through the lift. A majority of early faults like losing positioning on the 1st pull or not keeping the bar close are often due to not setting up correctly. FIX: Maintain good torso positioning by staying slow and smooth through the first pull and taking the time to make sure you're in the most ideal start position with the last engaged and bar tight to the shins. Common 2nd pull faults include missing contact with the hip entirely or hitting low on the legs which can result in a added space between the bar and the body and a loss of power. FIX: Slow down the first pull, aim to stay patient through the 2nd pull and work back from the Hang so you can continually dial in the correct position and timing. Faults like the catch and roll (holding the bar too tightly or not letting the hook grip soon enough in the Clean) or receiving the bar below the collar bone (recieving in a weak position, so you need to roll and stand to correct the fault). FIX: Focus on the "first touch" with the elbows high and hips back. Like most faults, if you fault here, fix the fault before standing. Working with lighter load can help develop the right timing. Common faults here are receiving with bent arms and pressing out after the catch is complete or catching the bar too far forward (limits the weight you can snatch) or too far back (which will dump the shoulders forward. FIX: Like all faults, own the receiving position before standing. Fixing faults in the receiving position reinforces the proper positioning when receiving the bar.

workouts.title: 🛠️ Introduction
workouts.description: In nearly all WODprep courses, we include a dedicated section called our Fault Fixer series. This series focuses on common movement mistakes and provides guidance on how to correct them. Specifically for WODprep Weightlifting, you’ll find videos addressing typical faults in lifts like the snatch, clean, and jerk. Each video breaks down the mistake and offers actionable tips to improve your technique. Click on any video in the section to explore a particular fault and learn strategies to correct it. The good news is that this library of Fault Fixers will continue to grow over time.

workouts.title: 🛠️ Soft Elbows / Rolled Shoulders [Snatch]
workouts.description: A common fault with the Snatch is soft elbows and rolled shoulders. That occurs when the Snatch is received with the arms not fully locked out or when the shoulders "dump" forward rather than being inline with the ears and torso. The elbows don't fully lock out and the bar is 'suspended' in air. The issue is we're supporting the bar with arm strength and not through a strong 'bone-on-bone" foundation. The head of the shoulder rolls forward and we get trapped in a weak overhead position. Extreme cases of rolled shoulder can expose the shoulder to unnecessary strain or injury. We want our Snatch receiving position with elbows locked, shoulders stacked, elbows and shoulders facing upwards with arm pits forward.

workouts.title: 🛠️ Slam and Swing [Snatch]
workouts.description: In trying to create power and speed, athletes will throw their hips to the bar causing the bar to swing out and away which can force them to jump forward to chase the it down. While a swing and slam can look "pretty good" in real time, the further the bar gets away from us the more power we lose. If you're an athlete who finds themselves jumping forward to catch a Snatch or experiencing a lot of pain through the hip pop, it's likely you've have some degree of Swing and Slam in your lift. Recording and reviewing video is one of the best ways to diagnose this fault, look for your shoulders in front of the bar with some bend at the waist through the 2nd pull.

workouts.title: 🛠️ Catch and Roll [Clean]
workouts.description: The Catch and Roll happens when we are unable to get into a proper front rack position when receiving a Clean because of a "death grip" the bar. Athletes who need to stand and roll the bar into position after the first touch are likely guilty of this fault. The Catch and Roll is a mistiming fault when the elbows coming through the transition before full hip extension is achieved. Missing extension forces you to hang onto the bar which can make for a difficult catch that can be hard on the wrists and elbows.

workouts.title: 🛠️ Early Arm Bend [Snatch, Clean]
workouts.description: "When the arm bends, the power ends" If the bar feels unnecessarily heavy or the transition to the shoulders or overhead feels sluggish or slow it's possible you're pulling the bar up with your arms before fully extending through the legs and hips. The role of the arms is to guide the bar into position and not to power it there. When we pull the bar early with the arms, it's likely we're missing that "moment" that will allows us to transition smoothly with the bar close and limiting our lift to what we can "hold".

workouts.title: 🛠️ Early Hip Rise [Snatch, Clean]
workouts.description: When hips lead the lift from the floor in the Snatch or Clean, it's difficult to drive upwards and hit optimal positions. Hips Rise Early This occurs when the hips initiate the drive and we lose the shoulder to hip angle from the floor. When the hips rise early it makes it difficult to get into a proper hang and power position but also means we have no leg drive left to get power the bar up vertically.

workouts.title: 🛠️ Lack of Full Extension [Snatch, Clean]
workouts.description: Muted or closed hips are another common fault that can limit lifting potential. Olympic lifting is super technical and it can feel like there are 300 things to remember to do in a lift. If you find you're failing to get your hips open when reviewing video or it's feeling like you're not moving as much weight as you could, like could be a very likely culprit. The goal is to stay long and tall through extension so we can create as much vertical momentum on the bar as possible.

workouts.title: 🛠️ Low Contact [Snatch, Clean]
workouts.description: A common fault in class and competitive settings is making low contact with the bar in the Snatch and Clean. When the bar makes low contact with the leg it indicates that we're rushing the to get to the lift and failing to get full extension, limiting the amount of drive we can extend through the lift.

workouts.title: 🛠️ Poor Dip [Jerk]
workouts.description: A poor dip in the push press, push jerk or split jerk is a major loss of power and as the weights get heavier, we'll need to drive as much momentum into the bar to lift the most weight overhead. A poor dip is limits that drive. Here, our weight moves forward, heels come up off the floor and our connection to the floor becomes "toesy". Feet stay flat but rather than staying vertical, we bend forward and drive the hips back as we initiate the dip. This can have major implications not only in the bar path but our ability to stay balanced under the bar and receive it in a strong overhead position. Dipping too deeply can not only stall the drive of the dip but can also cause a forward lean as the hips go back to squat. The most effective dip is short, straight and snappy. As you dip, the knees shoot inward and can cause a weakened drive.

workouts.title: 🛠️ Poor Receiving [Jerk]
workouts.description: Here are common faults we see when driving the bar off the shoulder in the jerk or receiving the bar overhead. A common fault with the spilt jerk as we shoot the hips back and lower the elbows when trying to create a more powerful drive. The more the bar gets away from a vertical line, the more power it loses and the more likely we need to chase it down before we can lock it out. Opposite to the previous fault, with the push jerk there is a tendency to lean back in the receiving position with the knees and hips forward of the shoulders. If the dip and drive is slow or if we not aggressive to the catch we'll end up catching the bar with bent elbows.
